judge_assessment.explanation: Both hard failures hold against the artifacts. Problem 2 ends "Explain in one sentence why this answer differs from your answer to problem 1 even though both use the 48 students in the same cell" and verify.json id 2 is a single probability check expecting 2/5. Problem 5 says "Show the two factors you multiplied, and state the conditional probability that the second factor represents" - three responses (5/12, 4/11 and the naming of P(second red | first red)) - and id 5 is one probability check expecting 5/33. Problem 6 asks the student to "State the total you divided by and why that total, not 200, is the correct denominator" and id 6 verifies only 2/5. Problem 7(b) asks the student to "state whether A and B are independent and justify the decision with your two numbers"; the two ids verify 0.2 and 0.5 but never the verdict (not independent). Problem 9 asks which term gives exactly two makes and "why that term carries a coefficient greater than 1"; id 9 is an expand check on (a+b)^3 alone. And verify.json holds exactly one manual entry, on id 10. Two additions the judge did not list: problem 1's "Write the conditional probability you are computing in P(A|B) notation before you divide" is an unverified printed response, and problem 3(c)'s actual answer is the independence verdict while the bank and the verify entry both hold the product 0.24. All probabilities recompute correctly against the table, including the independence result: P(sport)P(bus) = 0.6 x 0.4 = 0.24 = P(sport and bus), so the two events genuinely are independent.

strengths_to_preserve: The 200-student two-way table is arithmetically consistent in every margin (48+32=80, 72+48=120, 120+80=200) and is deliberately constructed so the events are exactly independent - 0.6 x 0.4 = 0.24 - which makes problem 3 a real test rather than a near miss the student has to judge by eye.

Problems 1 and 2 are the same 48-student cell read two ways, giving 3/5 and 2/5. Pairing P(A|B) against P(B|A) on identical data is the cheapest possible demonstration that conditioning direction matters, and the stem says so.

Problem 5's without-replacement draw (5/12 x 4/11 = 5/33) carries a declared trap at 25/144 for treating the draws as independent, so the general multiplication rule and the independent special case are distinguished by a concrete wrong number.

Problem 8 is a proper law-of-total-probability item built from realistic line yields (0.6 x 0.02 + 0.4 x 0.05 = 0.032), and it splits into (a) and (b) with separate answer lines and separate verify entries.

Problems 9 and 10 pair the symbolic binomial expansion with its numeric instance - the term 3a^2b is identified in problem 9 and evaluated as 3(0.8)^2(0.2) = 0.384 in problem 10 - so the coefficient 3 is met as a count before it is used as a multiplier.

root_causes.description: The per-id coverage rule lets a single probability check stand for a problem that prints a value plus a required explanation or a named factor. Problems 2, 5, 6, 7 and 9 each print more responses than the manifest covers, and the build still reports every problem verified.

improvements.title: Bind verification to every printed answer slot, not to one check per problem id
improvements.proposed_change: Count printed responses per problem. Here problem 5 prints three (the two factors and the conditional they represent), problem 6 prints two (the denominator 80 and the reason), problem 7(b) prints two (P(A|B) = 0.5 and the independence verdict), problem 3(c) prints two (the product 0.24 and the verdict), and problem 1 prints two (the P(A|B) notation and the value). Note that the sub-item structure is already machine-visible - this worksheet emits nine \ansline macros for its enumerated parts - so the counter has a reliable signal for the enumerated half and only needs prose heuristics for the rest.
improvements.regression_test: Add a tests/fixtures case with a two-slot problem: the worksheet prints "(a) find the value ... (b) write the rule" under one \problem id while verify.json carries a single entry for that id. A new answer-slot gate must exit non-zero naming the id and the uncovered slot. Today build.sh exits 0 on exactly this shape, so the test fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: The five flagged problems plus problems 1 and 3(c) move inside the boundary. Several of the missing responses are discrete and checkable (the denominator 80, the factors 5/12 and 4/11, the independence verdicts), so most of the gap closes with machine entries rather than manual ones.
improvements.risk: Slot counting from prose is heuristic; an over-eager counter could fail well-formed sheets. Mitigate by counting enumerated sub-parts and explicit "write ... on the answer line" phrases only, and by shipping the first release at exit 2 (manual review) rather than exit 1.

improvements.title: Require a manual entry whenever a problem asks the student to explain, name or justify
improvements.proposed_change: Require a manual entry whenever the stem asks the student to explain or justify. Problems 2 ('Explain in one sentence why'), 6 ('and why that total, not 200'), 7(b) ('justify the decision with your two numbers') and 9 ('explain why that term carries a coefficient greater than 1') each need one, with the model answer in desc so a grader has a target.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/check_manual_coverage.py plus a fixture whose problem stem contains an explain-class imperative (explain / justify / name the error / say in words / state whether) while its verify.json id has no entry of type manual. The gate must exit non-zero. I ran this exact lint over the ten cases in this shard: it fires on curr-402 (7 ids), curr-406 (4), curr-419 (5), curr-426 (2), curr-438 (5) and curr-450 (3), and stays silent on all three ACCEPTs (curr-413, curr-425, curr-432) - zero false positives. Fails before the fix, passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: The manual count rises from 1 to at least 5 and the build exits 2 naming them, so the delivered manifest matches what the sheet actually asks a human to read. This is the hard failure that drove instruction_following to 1.
improvements.risk: Verb-list linting will miss paraphrases ("what does that tell you about ...") and could nag on stems that merely narrate. Keep the list short, allow an explicit per-problem opt-out field in the JSON, and ship at exit 2 first.

case_summary: The probability is correct and the scenarios are well built - I checked every value against the table and the stems (3/5, 2/5, 3/5 and 6/25 versus 0.24, 0.9604, 5/33, 2/5, 0.2 versus 0.5, 0.012 and 0.032, the cubic expansion, 0.384) and found no error. The two-way table is deliberately constructed so the events are exactly independent, which makes problem 3 a real test. The failure is the shard's dominant one, and it bites harder here than elsewhere because conditional probability is a topic where the interpretation is the learning: five problems ask the student to explain a denominator, name a conditional factor, justify an independence decision or account for a binomial coefficient, and the manifest records ten probabilities and one manual entry. Everything the student is graded on beyond arithmetic sits outside the trust boundary. Notably the enumerated sub-parts already emit their own answer lines, so a slot-counting gate would have most of the signal it needs on this sheet without any prose parsing.
